main.text: [II, 524] ON THE ANIMALS OF SCRIPTURE PART TWO BOOK ONE ON ON THE CLEAN BIRDS. [col. 1]
CHAPTER I.
On the Hebrew name of the dove.

The sacred writers touch on the clean birds only briefly, with the single exception of the dove, about which they say more than about all the others taken together. It is therefore necessary to treat it more carefully. It is held that the dove is called in Hebrew יונה jona from the verb ינה jana, which means to oppress, as if it lay open to the plundering of all. On this point the poets are cited:
Censure pardons the ravens and harasses the doves.

This seems far-fetched. I shall therefore try to offer something more probable. In Jer 46:16 and L, 16. the Hebrew words מפני חרב היונה are rendered by the Greeks ἀπὸ προσώπου μαχαίρας Ἑλληνικῆς [apo prosōpou machairas Hellēnikēs], from the face of the Greek sword; by Jerome, from the face of the sword of the dove; by the Syriac, from the face of the sword ܡܣܝܒܐ [מסיבא] of the tormentor; by R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] and Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], האונסת, of the oppressor. But the Chaldee Paraphrast has מן קדם חרב סנאה דהיא כחמר מרויא, from the face of the hostile sword, which is like intoxicating wine, as if היונה were formed from יין, that is, from wine, with Yod and Vav interchanged. From the same source, then, יונה jona for the dove could be derived. If we follow this, יונה jona will properly be the οἰνὰς [oinas], a kind of wild dove so named from wine. 1. Because, on the authority of Eustathius, it is οἰνωπὸς τὸ χρῶμα [oinōpos to chrōma], that is, because it resembles wine, or ripe grapes, in colour. 2. Because it usually appears at the time of the vintage. Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 3: Οἰνὰς δὲ τοῦ [col. 2] φθινοπώρου καὶ φαίνεται μάλιστα, καὶ ἁλίσκεται· [Oinas de tou phthinopōrou kai phainetai malista, kai halisketai] The oenas (or, as Gaza renders it, vinago) appears and is caught chiefly in autumn. Athenaeus book 9, ch. 11: Ἡ δὲ φὰψ, καὶ ἡ περιστερὰ ἀεὶ φαίνονται· ἡ δὲ οἰνὰς φθινοπώρῳ μόνῳ· [Hē de phaps, kai hē peristera aei phainontai; hē de oinas phthinopōrō monō] The smaller wood pigeon and the dove are always to be seen; but the vinago only in autumn. But this etymology [II, 525] is contradicted by the usage of the Hebrews, among whom יונה jona, or יון jon, is not the οἰνὰς [oinas] but the dove in general, and properly the domestic one. Accordingly the οἰνὰς [oinas] dove was called by the Syrians ܟܪܡܝܘܢ [כרמיון] charmion, or ܟܪܡܝܘܢܐ [כרמיונא] charmiona, a word compounded of two, ܟܪܡ [כרם] and ܝܘܢ [יון], or ܝܘܢܐ [יונא], of which the former means vine and the latter dove. This was the very name of one of those famous handmaids of Cleopatra. In Greek it is written Χάρμιον [Charmion], or Χαρμιόνη [Charmionē], or Χαρμιουνώ [Charmiounō]. Plutarch in the Antony: Εἴρας ἡ Κλεοπάτρας κουρεύτρια, καὶ Χάρμιον, ὑφ᾽ ὧν τὰ μέγιστα διοικεῖται τῆς ἡγεμονίας· [Eiras hē Kleopatras koureutria, kai Charmion, hyph᾽ hōn ta megista dioikeitai tēs hēgemonias] Iras, Cleopatra's hairdresser, and Charmion, by whom the most important affairs of the realm were managed. And further on, regarding the death of Cleopatra: Τῶν δὲ γυναικῶν ἡ μὲν Εἴρας λεγομένη πρὸς τοῖς ποσὶν ἀπέθνησκεν· ἡ δὲ Χάρμιον, ἤδη σφαλλομένη, καὶ καρηβαροῦσα, κατεκόσμει τὸ διάδημα περὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῆς. [Tōn de gynaikōn hē men Eiras legomenē pros tois posin apethnēsken; hē de Charmion, ēdē sphallomenē, kai karēbarousa, katekosmei to diadēma peri tēn kephalēn autēs] Of her women, the one called Iras had died at her feet; Charmion, however, already tottering and heavy-headed, was adorning her head with the diadem. Galen, On theriac to Piso, book 1, chapter 8: Καὶ τοῖς ὀνόμασι λεγόμεναι Νάειρα, καὶ Καρμιόνη· ἡ μὲν ἀναπλέκουσα τὰς τρίχας εὐπρεπῶς, ἡ δὲ [col. 3] ἀποτέμνουσα τὰς ὑπεροχὰς τῶν ὀνύχων εὐφυῶς. [Kai tois onomasi legomenai Naeira, kai Karmionē; hē men anaplekousa tas trichas euprepōs, hē de apotemnousa tas hyperochas tōn onychōn euphyōs] And (Cleopatra's handmaids) called Naira and Carmione, of whom the former braided her hair becomingly, the latter skilfully trimmed the tips of her nails. Tzetzes, Chil. 6, Hist. 44:

Τῇ Κλεοπάτρᾳ τῇ σοφῇ, τῇ καὶ ὡραιοτάτῃ, Καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς δὲ σύμπασι ^{a)} πολλῶν ὑπερφερούσῃ, Πρὸς ἐπιμέλειαν τριχῶν, καὶ τῶν ὀνύχων, ἦσαν Χαρμιουνὼ, καὶ Τάειρα τί δε δηλοῦσι τάδε; Σύρον τὸν Τζέτζην βλέπε νῦν, Ἰσμαηλίτην ἅμα, Καὶ ταῦτα διαρθροῦντα σοι ταῖς γλώσσαις ταῖς ἐκείνων. Κατὰ Ἑβραίων γλῶσσάν τε, καὶ τὴν τῶν Σύρων ἅμα, Χαρμὶ δηλοῖ τὴν ἀμπελον, Οὐνὼ περιστεράν δε, Τὴν, ἣν ^{b)} φησιν οἱ Ἕλληνες περιστερὰν οἰνάδα, Κατὰ Ἰσμαηλίτας δὲ, τοὺς Ἄγαρ γόνους λέγω, Περιστερὰν τὴν Γάειραν σημαίνουσάν μοι νόει. [Tē Kleopatra tē sophē, tē kai hōraiotatē, / Kai tois loipois de sympasi ^{a)} pollōn hyperpherousē, / Pros epimeleian trichōn, kai tōn onychōn, ēsan / Charmiounō, kai Taeira ti de dēlousi tade? / Syron ton Tzetzēn blepe nyn, Ismaēlitēn hama, / Kai tauta diarthrounta soi tais glōssais tais ekeinōn. / Kata Hebraiōn glōssan te, kai tēn tōn Syrōn hama, / Charmi dēloi tēn ampelon, Ounō peristeran de, / Tēn, hēn ^{b)} phēsin hoi Hellēnes peristeran oinada, / Kata Ismaēlitas de, tous Agar gonous legō, / Peristeran tēn Gaeiran sēmainousan moi noei.]

Cleopatra, wise, most beautiful, and far surpassing all other women, had for the care of her hair and nails Charmiuno and Taïra. But what do these names signify? See now Tzetzes, at once a Syrian and an Ishmaelite, explaining them to you in their languages. In the language of the Hebrews as well as of the Syrians, Charmi signifies the vine, and Uno the dove, which the Greeks call the oenas dove. But among the Ishmaelites, I mean those descended from Hagar, understand that Taïra signifies [II, 526] the dove to me. From this gather that in Plutarch for Εἴρας [Eiras], and in Galen for Νάειρα [Naeira], one must write Τάειρας [Taeiras] or Τάειρα [Taeira], as in Tzetzes, who indeed writes this word correctly but interprets it wrongly. For the Arabic طاير [ṭāyir] taïr, or طايرة [ṭāyira] taira, does not signify a dove, but a bird in general. Hence for the Chaldeans טייר tajer means to take auguries. Nor should Charmiuno have been divided into Charmi and Uno, but into כרם charm and יונא juno. Meanwhile there is no doubt that Charmiuno, or Charmiona, is truly οἰνάς [oinas]. So יונה jona by itself is not οἰνὰς [oinas], but any dove. This being granted, no reason appears why יונה jona should be named from wine. Therefore something else must be sought. Nor perhaps will it be absurd to think that doves were called by their native name יונים jonim, as if Greek ones. For the Greeks were formerly called Ἴωνες [Iōnes] Iones, as we have proved elsewhere; and in Hebrew יונים jonim, with the same letters, although today they pronounce javanim, because that pleased the Masoretes. Two things chiefly suggest that doves were named from this. One, that in Pliny, book 10, chapter 29, Theophrastus reports that doves were imported into Asia. The other, that mythical history amply shows that there were doves in Greece from all time. Thus 1. they say that the Dodonaean dove ^{c)} ἱζομένην ἐπὶ φηγὸν, αὐδάξασθαι φωνῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ, ὡς χρεὼν εἴη, μαντήϊον αὐτόθι Διὸς γένεσθαι [hizomenēn epi phēgon, audaxasthai phōnē anthrōpinē, hōs chreōn eiē, mantēion autothi Dios genesthai], sitting on a beech tree, said with a human voice that it was fated that an oracle of Jupiter should be founded in that place, which was by far the most ancient of all Greece. 2. As from Noah, so from Deucalion they relate ^{d)} περιστερὰν, ἐκ τῆς λάρνακος ἀφιεμένην, δήλωμα γενέσθαι, χειμῶνος μὲν εἴσω πάλιν ἐνδυομένην, εὐδίας δὲ, ἀποπτᾶσαν [peristeran, ek tēs larnakos aphiemenēn, dēlōma genesthai, cheimōnos men eisō palin endyomenēn, eudias de, apoptasan], that a dove, sent out from the ark, was a sign of storm when it returned there, and of fair weather when it flew away. 3. Doves are said to have fed Jupiter, crying as an infant in Crete, with ambrosia brought from Ocean, according to Moero of Byzantium in Athenaeus, book 11,

Ζεὺς δ᾽ ἀρ᾽ ἐνὶ Κρήτῃ τρέφετο μέγας, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα τίς νιν Ἠήδει μακάρων. ὁ δ᾽ ἀέξετο πᾶσι μέλεσσι Τὸν μὲν ἄρα τρήρωνες ὑπὸ ζαθέῳ τρέφον ἄντρῳ, Ἀμβροσίην φορέουσαι ἀπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων. [Zeus d᾽ ar᾽ eni Krētē trepheto megas, oud᾽ ara tis nin ēēdei makarōn. ho d᾽ aexeto pasi melessi; ton men ara trērōnes hypo zatheō trephon antrō, ambrosiēn phoreousai ap᾽ Ōkeanoio rhoaōn.]

In Crete great Jupiter was nourished, and none of the Blessed knew him. And he grew in all his limbs. Doves, moreover, fed him in the divine cave, bringing ambrosia from the streams of Ocean. This is taken from Odyssey μ´ [12], where doves

— — ἀμβροσίην Διῒ πατρὶ φέρουσιν [ambrosiēn Dii patri pherousin], — — bring ambrosia to father Jupiter. [II, 527] Hence it is that in Plutarch's Symposium Cleodemus says to the poet Chersias: Εἰ τὴν [col. 4] ἀμβροσίαν τῷ Διῒ πελειάδες τινὲς κομίζουσιν, ὡς ὑμεῖς λέγετε [Ei tēn ambrosian tō Dii peleiades tines komizousin, hōs hymeis legete], If certain doves bring ambrosia to Jupiter, as you poets say. 4. At Aegium, a city of Achaea, Jupiter, changed into a dove, is said to have lain with the maiden Phthia. Athenaeus, book 9: Αὐτοκράτης ἐν τοῖς Ἀχαικοῖς καὶ τὸν Διὰ ἱστορεῖ μεταβαλεῖν τὴν μορφὴν εἰς περιστερὰν, ἐρασθέντα παρθένου Φθίας ὄνομα ἐν Αἰγείῳ [Autokratēs en tois Achaikois kai ton Dia historei metabalein tēn morphēn eis peristeran, erasthenta parthenou Phthias onoma en Aigeiō]. Autocrates in his Achaica relates that Jupiter himself, loving a maiden named Phthia in Aegium, changed his form into a dove. So too Aelian, Varia book 1, chapter 15. 5. The Argonauts, about to pass between the clashing Symplegades, were advised by the seer Phineus to send out a dove, and if it passed through them safely, they too should follow; and this they did. This dove is mentioned by Apollonius, book 2 of the Argonautica, Asclepiades, book 2 of the Τραγῳδούμενα [Tragōdoumena], Apollodorus, book 1 of the Bibliotheca, Hyginus, Fable 19, and not a few others. 6. When Ctesylla, daughter of Alcidamas of Ceos, who died in childbirth, was being carried out for burial, ἐκ τῆς στρομνῆς πελειὰς ἐξέπτη, καὶ τὸ σῶμα τῆς Κτησύλλης ἀφανὲς ἐγένετο [ek tēs stromnēs peleias exeptē, kai to sōma tēs Ktēsyllēs aphanes egeneto], a dove flew out of the bier, and the body of Ctesylla vanished. So Nicander, book 3 of the Ἑτεροιούμενα [Heteroioumena]. Hence Ovid, of Medea borne through the air, Metamorphoses book 7, Fable 12,
He passes also the walls of ancient Carthaea on Ceos, where the father Alcidamas was to marvel that a gentle dove could be born from the body of his daughter.
7. In the same author (Metam. book 13, Fable 4), the Oenotropae, daughters of Anius, as their father Anius tells Anchises,
— — — took on wings, and were turned into the snow-white birds of your consort, doves.

That is, into the birds of Venus, who had been the consort of Anchises. These stories, however fabulous, nevertheless serve our purpose. For from them you may at least gather that, in the opinion of those who invented these fables, there had always been doves in Greece. 8. What of the fact that Homer calls Boeotian Thisbe and Laconian Messene πολυτρήρωνας [polytērōnas], from their abundance of doves, Iliad 2? And Pliny, book 5, chapter 31, lists near Smyrna seven islands called Peristerides, that is, Columbariae [Dove Islands]. It is therefore very likely that after the Flood doves first made their way into Greece and the neighbouring places, and from there were gradually dispersed over the rest of the world.

You will say that these things are adduced in vain, since in those most ancient times after the Flood Syria too was πολυτρήρονα [polytērona], as is proved both from sacred and from profane histories. For in the sacred histories Abraham, than whom the Greeks have nothing more ancient, is commanded to offer to God a turtledove and a dove, Gen 15:9. And throughout the Law of Moses sacrifices of turtledoves and young doves are prescribed [II, 528]. For examples see Lev 1:14 and V, 7. 11. and XII, 6. and XIV, 22. and XXV, 14. 29. and Num 6:10. In the profane histories too, Semiramis, believed to be a contemporary of Abraham, is said to have been exposed in desert and rocky places near Ascalon, ἐν οἷς πολλοῦ πλήθους περιστερῶν ἐννοσσεύειν εἰωθότος, παραδόξως τροφῆς καὶ σωτηρίας τυχεῖν τὸ βρέφος [en hois pollou plēthous peristerōn ennosseuein eiōthotos, paradoxōs trophēs kai sōtērias tychein to brephos], where, since a great multitude of doves was accustomed to nest, the infant was wondrously fed and preserved. Indeed, the name of Semiramis is derived from the same source, as being κατὰ τὴν τῶν Σύρων διάλεκτον παρωνομασμένον ἀπὸ τῶν περιστερῶν [kata tēn tōn Syrōn dialekton parōnomasmenon apo tōn peristerōn], taken from doves in the language of the Syrians. So Diodorus, from Ctesias, in book 2. And R. Azarias [=Azariah de' Rossi, Meʾor ʿEnayim], in Meor Enajim, chapter 21, derives it from the word זמיר zemir, which denotes the song of birds, and specifically of the turtledove, Song 2:12. His words are as follows: נקראת סמיראמיס אשר לפי דבריו בלשון הארמי יורה על צפצוף העוף ולדעתי הוא מלשון עת הזמיר הגיע בחלוף הזין בסמך וכן בארמי פק דנטין זמרא דמנא זמרא דפומא ולזה אות דגלה היה יונה She is called Semiramis, which, according to his words, (that is, those of Diodorus, whom he had cited) signifies in the Syrian language the song of birds. This seems to be taken from the word זמיר zemir, as it is said in Song 2:12 [col. 5] "The time of zemir, that is, of song, has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land." For also in Syriac, in the Talmudic tractate Gittin, chapter 1, זמרא דמנא zemara demana is instrumental music, and זמרא דפומא zemara dephuma vocal music. And therefore Semiramis had a dove as the emblem of her banner. Indeed, he contends in what follows that not only Semiramis but all the kings of Assyria had a dove as the symbol of their banners. And that this is why, for the wrath and sword of the Assyrians, Jeremiah had said חרון היונה, the wrath of the dove, Jer 25:38 and חרב היונה, the sword of the dove, Jer 46:16, and L, 16. This he confirms from the version of Jerome and from the Commentaries of Thomas Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)] on Jeremiah. To the same he also refers the fact that Jerusalem in Zeph 3:1 is called היונה, the dove, as if the Prophet were reproaching her שהיא במעשיו דומה לבבל אשר אות דגלה יונה, that in her deeds she is like Babylon, which had a dove on its banner as its military emblem. And following him, R. David Ganz, in book 2 of his Chronology, at the year 1958: The emblem of the banner of Semiramis was the figure of a dove. This banner emblem all the kings of Assyria imitated. Hence Jeremiah, chapter XXV, verse 28: "Because of the wrath of the dove"; and chapter XLVI, verse 6: "Before the sword of the dove". To this the ancients add that Semiramis was changed into a dove. Diodorus, in the place cited above: Ἔνιοι δὲ μυθολογοῦντές φασιν αὐτὴν γενέσθαι περιστερὰν, καὶ πολλῶν ὀρνέων εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν καταπετασθέντων, μετ᾽ ἐκείνων ἐκπετασθῆναι· [Enioi de mythologountes phasin autēn genesthai peristeran, kai pollōn orneōn eis tēn oikian katapetasthentōn, met᾽ ekeinōn ekpetasthēnai] But others tell the fable that she became a dove, and that when many birds had flown into the house, she flew away with them. Ovid, Metam. book 4, Fable 2, where, concerning her mother Derceto,

Or rather, that, having taken wings from that daughter of hers, she spent her last years in lofty towers? [II, 529] Lucian in De Syria Dea: Τὸ Σεμιράμιος τέλος εἰς περιστερὰν ἀπίκετο [To Semiramios telos eis peristeran apiketo], Semiramis was at last turned into a dove. Athenagoras, in the Legatio, on the same woman: Τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον, εἰς περιστερὰν μετέβαλεν ἡ γυνή· ὁ μύθος παρὰ Κτησίᾳ [To gar adynaton, eis peristeran metebalen hē gynē; ho mythos para Ktēsia]. For, what is impossible, the woman was changed into a dove. The tale is found in Ctesias. This is why among the Syrians and Assyrians doves were held in great veneration, as Ctesias teaches in Diodorus, after relating that Semiramis was nourished by doves and also took her name from them: Ἃς ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνων τῶν χρόνων, οἱ κατὰ Συρίαν ἅπαντες διετέλεσαν, ὡς Θεὰς τιμῶντες [Has ap᾽ ekeinōn tōn chronōn, hoi kata Syrian hapantes dietelesan, hōs Theas timōntes]; These, from those times on, all the Syrians have never ceased to worship as goddesses. And after the story of her metamorphosis into a dove the same author adds: Διὸ καὶ τοὺς Ἀσσυρίους τὴν περιστερὰν τιμᾷν ὡς Θεὸν, ἀπαθανατίζοντες τὴν Σεμίραμιν [Dio kai tous Assyrious tēn peristeran timan hōs Theon, apathanatizontes tēn Semiramin]; Hence the Assyrians also venerate the dove as a goddess, in order to rescue Semiramis from death. Xenophon too, in book 1 of the Cyrus the Younger, speaking of the fish of the Chalus, a river of Syria: Οὓς οἱ Σύροι Θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον, καὶ ἀδικεῖν οὐκ εἴων, οὐδὲ τὰς περιστεράς [Hous hoi Syroi Theous enomizon, kai adikein ouk eiōn, oude tas peristeras]. These the Syrians regarded as gods, and forbade anyone to harm them, as also the doves. Philo in Eusebius, near the end of book 8 of the Praeparatio Evangelica: Ἀμήχανόν τι πελειάδων πλῆθος ἐπὶ τῶν τριόδων, καὶ κατ᾽ οἰκίαν ἑκάστην, ἐθεασάμην. πυνθανομένῳ δέ μοι τὴν αἰτίαν ἔφασαν, οὐ θεμιτὸν εἶναι συλλαμβάνειν. ἀπειρῆσθαι γὰρ ἐκ παλαίου τοῖς οἰκήτορσι τὴν χρῆσιν [Amēchanon ti peleiadōn plēthos epi tōn triodōn, kai kat᾽ oikian hekastēn, etheasamēn. pynthanomenō de moi tēn aitian ephasan, ou themiton einai syllambanein. apeirēsthai gar ek palaiou tois oikētorsi tēn chrēsin]. I saw an immense multitude of doves at the crossroads and in every house (at Ascalon). And when I asked the reason, they answered that it was unlawful to catch them, for their use had long ago been forbidden to the inhabitants. Tibullus, Elegy 8:
The white dove, sacred to the man of Palestine.

Al. Syro, or suo. Hyginus, Fab. 197: the Syrians regard fish and doves as among the gods; they do not eat them. Lucian, in the place cited above, on the Hierapolitans: Ὀρνίθων τε αὐτέοισι περιστερὴ δοκέει χρῆμα ἱρώτατον, καὶ οὐδὲ ψαύειν αὐτέων δικαιεῦσι· [Ornithōn te auteoisi peristerē dokeei chrēma hirōtaton, kai oude psauein auteōn dikaieusi] Among birds the dove seems to them the most sacred, and they do not think it right even to touch it. Likewise: Ὄρνιθας τοὺς μὲν ἄλλους σιτέονται· περιστερὴν δὲ μούνην οὐ σιτέονται, ἀλλὰ σφίσι ἥδε ἱερή. [Ornithas tous men allous siteontai; peristerēn de mounēn ou siteontai, alla sphisi hēde hierē] [col. 6] They eat other birds, but abstain from the dove alone, which is sacred to them. Phornutus [=L. Annaeus Cornutus, De natura deorum], in the book On the Gods, in the chapter on Rhea: Ἔοικε δὲ ἡ αὐτὴ ἡ παρὰ Σύροις Ἄρταγα εἶναι, ἣν διὰ τὸ περιστερὰς καὶ ἰχθύος ἀπέχεσθαι τιμῶσι· [Eoike de hē autē hē para Syrois Artaga einai, hēn dia to peristeras kai ichthyos apechesthai timōsi] She seems to be the same as the one whom the Syrians call Artaga (others Atergatis and Derceto) and whom they worship by abstaining from fish and the dove. Clement of Alexandria in the Protrepticus: Οὐδέ γε τῶν τὴν Φοινίκην Σύρων κατοικούντων (ἐκλήσομαι) ὧν οἱ μὲν τὰς περιστερὰς, οἱ δὲ τοὺς ἰχθῦς οὕτω σέβουσι περιττῶς, ὡς Ἠλεῖοι τὸν Δία· [Oude ge tōn tēn Phoinikēn Syrōn katoikountōn (eklēsomai) hōn hoi men tas peristeras, hoi de tous ichthys houtō sebousi perittōs, hōs Ēleioi ton Dia] Nor shall I forget the Syrians who live in Phoenicia, some of whom worship doves, others fish, as fervently as the Eleans worship Jupiter. Meor enajim: ונמצאו קצת אמות שבכה אהבו את זכר סמיראמיס ואות דגלה שאסרו על עצמן לאכול את בני היונה And certain nations were found who so revered the memory of Semiramis and the [II, 530] emblem of her banner that they forbade themselves to eat doves. Nor were the Samaritans free from this superstition, if indeed we believe the Jews. The Talmud, tractate Cholin, ch. 1, fol. 6a, on the Cuthaeans or Samaritans: אמר רב נחמן בר יצחק דמות יונה מצאו להן בראש הר גריזים שהיו עובדין אותה Said Rab Nachman, son of Isaac: they found among them the image of a dove, which they worshipped on Mount Gerizim. The gloss on the Talmudic tractate Avodazera, fol. 26b: אל ימול כותי שמל לשם דמות שנמצאו בראש הר גריזים ועובדין לה עבודה כדאמר בהכל שיחטין ומלו את בניהם לשם יונה זו, A Cuthaean shall not circumcise, for he circumcises in the name of the image which they found on the summit of Mount Gerizim, and they worship it, as is related in the chapter (of Cholin, cited above, which begins) "All slaughter": and they circumcise their sons in the name of this dove. Meor enajim: קרוב בעיני להאמין שהכותיים אשר הושיב מלך אשור ובבל בשומרון לאות ולעד הכנעם באהבה אל מלכם ההוא אשר אות דגלה יונה חבבו אותה והקימוהו ליראתם בראש הר גריזים אשר עם שכם ראש ממלכת שומרון בימים ההם, I am fully persuaded that the Cuthaeans, whom the king of Assyria and Babylonia had deported to Samaria, as a sign and testimony of their love and devotion toward their king, who had the dove as the emblem of his banner, loved the dove, and erected a statue, which they worshipped, on the summit of Mount Gerizim, near the city of Shechem, which was then the capital of the Samaritan kingdom. Tsemach David, in the Chronology of the Second Temple, at the year 881: In the days of R. Meir they found the Cuthaeans' image of a dove on Mount Gerizim, as is stated in the first chapter of Cholin. And he decreed that they should be treated in every respect as gentiles of the land. ^{R1}.

From this it might seem possible to conclude that doves have nested in Syria as well as in Greece from all time. Yet there is an objection to be raised: in the age of Moses, it is true, בני יונה, young of doves, were offered even by common people in Israel, as the Law expressly prescribes; but whether Abraham offered the same can be called into question. For we do not read that he offered תור ובן יונה, a turtledove and a young dove, as is commanded [II, 531] in the Law of Moses, but תור וגוזל, a turtledove and a gozal. This word signifies not only the young of the dove properly so called, but also the young of the turtledove, of the wood pigeon, of the livia, of the vinago, and of any other bird that may be assigned to the dove kind. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter On القطا [al-qaṭā] alkata, as the Arabs call a certain kind of wood pigeon, writes: يقال القطا والحمام وانواعها امهات الجوازل والجوازل فراخها الواحد جوزل [yuqāl al-qaṭā wa-l-ḥamām wa-anwāʿuhā ummahāt al-jawāzil wa-l-jawāzil firākhuhā al-wāḥid jawzal] "Alkata and the dove, and [col. 7] birds of the same kind are called the mothers of the algavvazil. And the algavvazil are their young, from the singular gauzal." Now جوزل [jawzal] gauzal is for the Arabs exactly what גוזל gozal is for the Hebrews. Accordingly, since there are various species of gozal, when a pipio [squab] is meant precisely, there is sometimes added, by way of distinction, "gozal, young of the dove." Thus in the Chaldee paraphrast of the Song of Songs, chapter 1, verse 15: "Your eyes are כגוזלין בני יונתא, like gozalin, young of the dove." And Vajikra Rabba [=Leviticus Rabbah], chapter 22, on the emperor Titus: קראו לרופאים ומצאו בו כמו גוזל בן יונה והיה בו משקל שתי לטראות, "They called the physicians, who (when his skull had been cut open) found in it something like a gozal, a young of the dove, weighing two pounds." It is called gozal, or gauzal, from its peeping, just as in Latin pipio. For الجزل [al-jazl] algezel is pipitus [peeping]. In the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] it is rendered صوت الحمام [ṣawt al-ḥamām] the voice of the dove, namely of one still peeping and not yet grown. Therefore those are mistaken who derive גוזל gozal from the verb גזל gazal, that is, to seize, because it is exposed to plunder. The Syrians, by metathesis, say ܙܘܓܠ [זוגל] zogal instead of ܓܘܙܠ [גוזל] gozal. But the Phoenicians of old said gozol. Hence peristereon is in Punic חציר־גוזול azirgozol, that is, herb of the squab, in the Herbarium of Apuleius, chapter 65.

Now, the same objection could be raised regarding the doves of Semiramis. For although the later Syrians also worshipped יונים jonim, that is, domestic doves, those properly so called, out of regard for Semiramis, it nevertheless seems possible to infer, even from Ctesias, that wild doves were attendant on her. For he calls the places in which those doves lived desert and rocky, ἐρήμους, καὶ πετρώδεις τόπους [erēmous, kai petrōdeis topous]. Accordingly the name of Semiramis, taken from this, is explained by Hesychius as περιστερὰ ὄρειος [peristera oreios], mountain dove. We have shown elsewhere that this word is Arabic, not Syrian as is supposed, and that it was written Serimam, which the Greeks changed διὰ τὴν εὐφωνίαν [dia tēn euphōnian] into Σεμίραμιν [Semiramin]. For among the Arabs حمام [ḥmām] himam is dove, and سراة [srāh] sera mountain, شعرا [shʿrā] sera forest, صحرا [ṣḥrā] sahra desert; from some one of these words joined with حمام [ḥmām] himam the name Serimam was formed, for dove of the mountain, or of the forest, or of the desert. Such is the composition in the words כרמיון charmion or כרמיונא charmiona, of which we have spoken, and חריונים chirjonim or דביונים dibjonim, of [II, 532] which we shall speak. But the chief point is this: from the history of Semiramis it can in no way be proved that doves were already worshipped in Syria in ancient times, because her date is quite uncertain. For if we follow Ctesias, a highly fabulous writer, Semiramis was the wife of Ninus, whose reign would fall in the times of Abraham. But others make Semiramis the daughter of Belochus, who was more than five hundred years later than Ninus. Hence Eusebius at the number 582, which is the tenth year from the death of Joshua: Eighteenth king of the Assyrians, Belochus, for 25 years; whose daughter Atossa, who is also Semiramis, reigned with her father for 12 years. And Photius, on author 186, concerning the Canon, Hist. 9: Ὅσα οἱ ἄλλοι περὶ Ἀττόσης Ἀσσυρίου ἀναγράφουσι, ταῦθ᾽ οὗτος εἰς Σεμίραμιν ἀναφέρει· [Hosa hoi alloi peri Attosēs Assyriou anagraphousi, tauth᾽ houtos eis Semiramin anapherei] Whatever others write about Atossa the Assyrian, he refers to Semiramis. But, what is more surprising, if we believe Herodotus in his first book, Semiramis was older only by πέντε γενεαῖς [pente geneais], five generations, that is, at most two hundred years, than Nitocris, the mother of that Labonitus whom Cyrus defeated. Yet between Cyrus and Belochus more than a thousand years intervene, and between him and Ninus fifteen or sixteen hundred. Nor can the deeds of Semiramis be referred to the age of Abraham, when, as may be gathered from Gen. XIV, the king of שנער, or Babylonia, was a petty prince. And equally uncertain is what some assert, that the kings of Babylonia had the dove [col. 8] as a military standard, since no ancient author is cited who reports this ^{R2}. And it is most probable that Cyrus, after subjecting the Babylonians to his rule, adopted the same military standards that his predecessors, the Medes and Assyrians, had had. But that he had an eagle as his standard is clear from these words of Xenophon in the seventh book of the Cyropaedia: Ἦν δ᾽ αὐτῷ τὸ σημεῖον ἀετὸς χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ δόρατος μακροῦ ἀνατεταμένος [Ēn d᾽ autō to sēmeion aetos chrysous epi doratos makrou anatetamenos]. His standard was a golden eagle, stretched out upon a long spear. This all the kings of the Persians thereafter imitated. The same Xenophon: Καὶ νῦν δὲ ἔτι τοῦτο τὸ σημεῖον τῷ Περσῶν βασιλεῖ διαμένει· [Kai nyn de eti touto to sēmeion tō Persōn basilei diamenei] This standard still remains even today for the king of the Persians. Curtius, book 3, on the army of Darius: Among these they had consecrated a golden eagle, resembling one spreading its wings. Philostratus in the Heroica, in the chapter on Themistocles: Μῆδοι ταῦτα, καὶ Βαβυλὼν μέση, καὶ τὸ σημεῖον τὸ βασίλειον ὁ χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ τῆς πέλτης ἀετός· [Mēdoi tauta, kai Babylōn mesē, kai to sēmeion to basileion ho chrysous epi tēs peltēs aetos] These things are the Medes, and Babylon in the middle, and the military standard, a golden eagle upon a spear. Therefore in Jeremiah [XXV, 38. XLVI,16. L,16.] חרב היונה is not, as I at least think, the sword of the dove, but the oppressing or devastating sword, such as that of the Babylonians was under King Nebuchadnezzar ^{R3}. Accordingly [II, 533] the prophet says of the same, Jer 46:14: אכלה חרב סביביך, The sword has devoured round about you. But that the Samaritans also worshipped doves is entirely fabulous. What idols they worshipped when they were first transplanted from Assyria into Samaria is related in 2 Reg. XVII, 30. 31.: The men of Babylon made Succoth-Benoth, the Cuthites made Nergal, etc. But there the Sacred History says not a γρῦ [gry] about a dove, or its image, worshipped by them. Nor was this anywhere charged against them by Josephus, who in many places inveighs sharply against them. See the ninth book of the Jewish Antiquities, and the end of the eleventh; and chapters 1 and 7 of book 12; and chapter 6 of book 13; and chapters 3 and 5 of book 18; and chapter 5 of book 20. Nor could the worship of the dove, or of its image, in any way have been consistent with the Law of Moses, which they accepted. For, to say nothing of the fact that all images are forbidden so often and so expressly by Moses, on what pretext could they possibly have worshipped the very animal which they were commanded to slaughter to God in sacrifice? Nevertheless it is undoubtedly true, as Xenophon, Ctesias, Lucian and other eyewitnesses, αὐτόπται [autoptai], assert, that the Syrians and Assyrians either worshipped doves as goddesses, or at least abstained from them as from something sacred. But at what precise time this superstition was introduced into Syria or Assyria, no one could easily say.

notes.text: That the dove was given the name יונה because it had been brought from Greece into Asia seems hardly probable. For what Bochart proves with a great display of learning, that doves are mentioned in Greece from all time past, is irrelevant to the matter. Does it follow from this that doves were native to no other region, or that they were brought from Greece into Asia? I am therefore surprised that this opinion pleased Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], so much that he even adorned it with new arguments, in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] vol. 4, p. 1094 ff. I would think that the dove was given its name from its gentleness, a notion present in the Arabic verbs أَانَ [ʾāna] and هَانَ [hāna], whence أون [ʾawn] is mildness, affability, and هون [hawn] gentleness, mildness, so that it corresponds in a way to the Chaldee הון, rest, ease. Other conjectures on the reason for that name will be given by Simonis in the Arcanum Formarum, p. 42.
